questions.subject: companies-act
questions.stem: In a public company, if a quorum is not present within half an hour of the time appointed for a general meeting (not called on requisition of members), the meeting:

steps: s.103(2)(a): meeting stands adjourned to the same day next week, same time and place, or other date/time/place determined by the Board.
Only at the adjourned meeting do the members present constitute the quorum (s.103(3)).
explanation.formula_used: s.103(2): no quorum in 30 minutes → adjourned one week (or as Board fixes)
explanation.trap: 'Members present are the quorum' applies only at the adjourned meeting.

options.text: Stands dissolved and must be called afresh by a new notice of 21 clear days to members
options.error: requisition-meeting cancellation rule applied to all meetings
options.label: A

options.text: Stands adjourned to the same day next week, same time and place, or as the Board fixes
options.label: B

options.text: Proceeds at once, the members present being deemed to constitute the quorum for it
options.error: adjourned-meeting rule applied to the original meeting
options.label: C

options.text: Stands adjourned to the same day in the next month, same time and place, or as fixed
options.label: D

questions.subject: companies-act
questions.stem: Kamal Chemicals Ltd, a public company, has 3,200 members. Its AGM fails for want of quorum and the Board fixes the adjourned meeting on a date other than the same day of the next week. Which is correct?

steps: s.103(1)(a)(ii): public company with more than 1,000 but up to 5,000 members → 15 members personally present.

s.103(2) proviso: if adjourned to a different date/time/place, at least 3 days' notice to members individually or by advertisement in newspapers (one English, one vernacular) circulating where the registered office is situated.
explanation.formula_used: Quorum 5 / 15 / 30 (≤1,000 / ≤5,000 / >5,000 members); 3 days' notice for a re-fixed adjourned meeting
explanation.trap: Only a change from the default 'same day next week' triggers the 3-day notice.

options.text: Quorum 15 members personally present; a fresh notice of 21 clear days to all members
options.error: adjourned meeting treated as a new meeting
options.label: A

options.text: Quorum 5 members personally present; 3 days' notice, individually or by advertisement
options.error: quorum band for up to 1,000 members applied
options.label: B

options.text: Quorum 15 members personally present; 3 days' notice, individually or by advertisement
options.label: C

options.text: Quorum 30 members personally present; 3 days' notice, individually or by advertisement
options.error: quorum band for more than 5,000 members applied
options.label: D

questions.subject: companies-act
questions.stem:
Vinayak Steel Ltd, a public company with 6,000 members, calls its AGM. Consider:

1. The quorum is 30 members personally present.
2. If the meeting is adjourned for want of quorum and, at the adjourned meeting, a quorum is again not present within half an hour, the 4 members present shall be the quorum.
3. Had the meeting been called on the requisition of members under s.100 and quorum been absent, it would stand cancelled.

Which of the statements are correct?

steps: s.103(1)(a)(iii): more than 5,000 members → 30 members.
s.103(3): at the adjourned meeting, if quorum absent within half an hour, members present shall be the quorum.
s.103(2)(b): a meeting called on requisition under s.100 stands cancelled.
explanation.trap: There is no minimum number at the adjourned meeting — whoever is present is the quorum.

options.error: quorum band for more than 5,000 members misapplied
options.label: A

questions.subject: companies-act
questions.stem: Under s.196(3), a company shall not appoint or continue the employment of a person as managing director, whole-time director or manager who is below the age of ____ or has attained the age of ____ (the latter subject to a special resolution exception).

steps: s.196(3)(a): below 21 or attained 70 years — barred; appointment of a person above 70 is possible by special resolution with justification in the explanatory statement.
explanation.formula_used: MD/WTD/manager: 21 ≤ age < 70 (70+ by special resolution)
explanation.trap: 75 is the SEBI LODR trigger for non-executive directors, not the Companies Act MD limit.

options.error: SEBI LODR non-executive director age (75) used
options.label: A

options.error: age of majority used for the lower limit
options.label: B

questions.subject: companies-act
questions.stem: Mr Venkat, aged 71, is proposed as a Whole-time Director of Nilgiri Tea Ltd, a public company. Which is correct?

steps: s.196(3)(a) proviso: a person who has attained 70 may be appointed by special resolution; the explanatory statement must indicate the justification.
explanation.formula_used: Age 70+ → special resolution + justification in explanatory statement
explanation.trap: The bar at 70 is not absolute.

options.text: He cannot be appointed at all, since he has already attained the age of 70 years
options.label: A

options.text: He may be appointed by special resolution, with justification in the explanatory statement
options.label: B

options.text: Central Government approval is needed in every case, in addition to a special resolution
options.label: C

options.text: An ordinary resolution suffices, provided the Board recommends his appointment
options.label: D

questions.subject: companies-act
questions.stem:
Consider the following about alternate directors under s.161(2):

1. The Board may appoint one only if authorised by the articles or by a resolution passed in general meeting.
2. The original director must be absent from India for a period of not less than three months.
3. A person who is already a director of the same company may be appointed as the alternate.

Which are correct?

steps: s.161(2): Board may appoint (if authorised by articles or GM resolution) an alternate for a director absent from India for not less than three months.
No person holding an alternate directorship for any other director, or holding a directorship in the same company, can be appointed.
explanation.formula_used: Alternate: authorisation + ≥3 months' absence from India + not already a director/alternate in the company
explanation.trap: Absence from meetings is not enough — absence from India is the trigger.

options.error: bar on existing directors acting as alternate overlooked
options.label: C

questions.subject: companies-act
questions.stem: Ms Kavya, an independent director of Orbit Ltd, leaves India on 1 August 2026 for five months. The Board (authorised by the articles) appoints Mr Jatin as her alternate. Ms Kavya returns to India early, on 15 October 2026. Which is correct?

steps: s.161(2) proviso: an alternate for an independent director must be qualified to be appointed as an independent director.
The alternate holds office no longer than permissible to the original director and vacates when the original director returns to India.
explanation.formula_used: Alternate vacates on return of original director; alternate for an ID must be ID-qualified
explanation.trap: Early return ends the alternate's tenure immediately.

options.text: Jatin must meet the s.149(6) criteria, and he vacates office on Kavya's return on 15 October 2026
options.label: A

options.text: Jatin need not meet s.149(6) criteria, since he only substitutes for Kavya during her absence
options.label: B

options.text: Jatin continues in office until Kavya's originally planned five-month absence ends
options.error: vacation on return of original director overlooked
options.label: C

options.text: Jatin holds office until the next AGM, like an additional director appointed by the Board
options.label: D

questions.subject: companies-act
questions.stem: Under s.423, an appeal against an order of the NCLAT lies to the Supreme Court:

steps: s.423: any person aggrieved may appeal to the Supreme Court within 60 days from receipt of the order, on any question of law.
The Supreme Court may allow a further period not exceeding 60 days on sufficient cause.
explanation.formula_used: s.423: 60 days + up to 60 days; questions of law only
explanation.trap: Facts are settled at the NCLAT; only law goes up.

options.text: Within 30 days of receipt of the order, on any question arising
options.error: IBC-type window and unrestricted scope assumed
options.label: A

options.text: Within 45 days of receipt of the order, on questions of fact and law
options.error: NCLAT appeal window and scope applied
options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D

questions.subject: companies-act
questions.stem: A certified copy of an NCLAT order is received by Mehul on 3 March 2026. If the Supreme Court is satisfied that he had sufficient cause for delay, the latest date up to which it may entertain his appeal is:

steps: Normal window: 60 days from receipt → 2 May 2026.
Further period (sufficient cause): not exceeding 60 days → 1 July 2026.
explanation.formula_used: SC appeal: 60 + 60 days from receipt of NCLAT order
explanation.trap: The extension equals the original window (60), unlike NCLAT's 45 + 45.

options.error: NCLAT's 45-day extension applied to the Supreme Court
options.label: C

questions.subject: companies-act
questions.stem: An appeal to the NCLAT against an order of the NCLT under the Companies Act must be filed within:

steps: s.421(3): 45 days from the date on which a copy of the order is made available; NCLAT may entertain within a further period not exceeding 45 days if satisfied of sufficient cause.
explanation.trap: IBC appeals (30 + 15) run on a different clock.

options.text: 45 days from availability of the order copy, plus up to 45 days for sufficient cause
options.label: A

options.text: 90 days from availability of the order copy, with no further extension allowed
options.label: B

options.text: 60 days from availability of the order copy, plus up to 60 days for sufficient cause
options.label: C

questions.subject: companies-act
questions.stem:
Consider the following about appeals from the NCLT:

1. No appeal lies to the NCLAT from an order of the NCLT made with the consent of the parties.
2. After hearing the parties, the NCLAT may confirm, modify or set aside the order and sends a copy of its order to the NCLT and the parties.
3. Only the company that was a party before the NCLT may appeal; other aggrieved persons cannot.

Which are correct?

steps: s.421(1): any person aggrieved by an NCLT order may appeal → 3 wrong.
s.421(2): no appeal from an order made with the consent of parties → 1 correct.
s.421(4): NCLAT passes orders confirming, modifying or setting aside, and sends copies → 2 correct.
explanation.trap: Consent orders are final by design.

options.error: 'any person aggrieved' misread as only the company
options.label: B

questions.subject: companies-act
questions.stem: The copy of an NCLT order was made available to Rudra Ltd on 12 January 2026. Rudra files its appeal before the NCLAT on 20 March 2026. The appeal is:

steps: Days from 12 January 2026 to 20 March 2026 = 67.
Normal limit 45 days; further period up to 45 days (outer limit 90) only on sufficient cause.
explanation.formula_used: s.421(3): 45 days as of right; 46–90 days only on sufficient cause
explanation.trap: The extra 45 days is discretionary, not a right.

options.text: Filed on day 67: time-barred, since the outer limit including any extension is only 60 days
options.error: Supreme Court's 60-day window confused with NCLAT's outer limit
options.label: A

options.text: Filed on day 67: within time, since a 90-day period is available to the appellant as of right
options.label: B

options.text: Filed on day 67: late, but within the further 45 days; NCLAT may admit it on sufficient cause
options.label: C

options.text: Filed on day 67: time-barred, since the NCLAT has no power at all to condone any delay
options.error: condonation power of s.421(3) proviso overlooked
options.label: D

questions.subject: companies-act
questions.stem:
Before recommending an auditor, the Audit Committee (or the Board, where no committee is required) must, under the Audit and Auditors Rules, take into consideration:

1. The qualifications and experience of the individual or firm.
2. Whether those qualifications and experience are commensurate with the size and requirements of the company.
3. Any order or pending proceeding relating to professional matters of conduct against the proposed auditor before ICAI or any competent authority or court.
4. Whether the proposed auditor has quoted the lowest fee.

Select the correct answer:

steps: Rule 3(2), Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules 2014: qualifications and experience; commensurability with size and requirements; pending orders/proceedings on professional conduct.
Lowest fee is not a statutory criterion; s.139(1) also requires the auditor's written consent and eligibility certificate.
explanation.formula_used: Rule 3: qualifications, commensurability, disciplinary history
explanation.trap: Price is not a statutory selection criterion.

source_refs.note: Companies Act 2013 s.139(1),(11); Rule 3, Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules 2014

questions.subject: companies-act
questions.stem: Where the Companies Act requires a valuation of shares, property or net worth, the registered valuer is appointed by:

steps: s.247(1): valuation by a registered valuer appointed by the Audit Committee or, in its absence, by the Board.
IBBI is the authority that registers valuers under the Registered Valuers Rules 2017.
explanation.formula_used: s.247(1): AC → else Board
explanation.trap: IBBI registers valuers; it does not appoint them for a company.

options.text: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India, as registering authority
options.error: registering authority confused with appointing authority
options.label: A

options.text: The members of the company by ordinary resolution in general meeting
options.error: appointing authority confused with statutory auditor
options.label: B

options.text: The Board of Directors in all cases, irrespective of any committee
options.label: C

options.text: The Audit Committee or, in its absence, the Board of Directors
options.label: D

questions.subject: companies-act
questions.stem:
Mr Naresh, a registered valuer, is engaged in May 2026 to value the shares of Pioneer Ltd, an unlisted company, for a preferential allotment. Consider:

1. He cannot undertake the valuation if he was interested in the shares at any time during the three years before his appointment.
2. He must not become interested in the shares for three years after the valuation.
3. For a preferential issue under s.62(1)(c), the price must be determined on the basis of a registered valuer's report.
4. If the Audit Committee cannot meet, the Managing Director alone may appoint him.

Select the correct answer:

steps: s.247(2)(c): no valuation of an asset in which the valuer has direct/indirect interest, or becomes interested, during 3 years before appointment or 3 years after valuation.
s.62(1)(c): price determined by the valuation report of a registered valuer (unlisted company).
s.247(1): appointment by AC, else Board — not by the MD alone.
explanation.formula_used: s.247: 3 years before + 3 years after; AC/Board appoints
explanation.trap: The interest bar runs both backwards and forwards.

options.error: MD treated as an appointing authority
options.label: D

questions.stem: Under ss.153–155, a Director Identification Number is:

steps: s.153: application to the Central Government; s.154: allotment within one month.
s.155: no individual who has been allotted a DIN shall apply for or obtain another.
explanation.formula_used: One individual, one DIN (s.155)
explanation.trap: The DIN travels with the person, not the company.

options.text: Allotted separately for each company in which the individual is a director
options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D

questions.subject: companies-act
questions.microtopic_name: Appointment, DIN and intimation to the Registrar
questions.stem: Rewa Ltd appoints Ms Tara as a director on 5 August 2026. The last date for filing the return of particulars of the appointment with the Registrar is:

steps: s.170(2): return with particulars of appointment/change of directors and KMP within 30 days.
5 August 2026 + 30 days = 4 September 2026.
explanation.trap: The consent filing under s.152(5) runs on the same 30-day clock.

questions.subject: companies-act
questions.microtopic_name: Appointment, rotation and tenure of auditors
questions.stem:
Which of the following companies are covered by the auditor-rotation requirement of s.139(2)?

(a) An unlisted public company with paid-up capital of ₹8 crore and no borrowings.
(b) A private company with paid-up capital of ₹60 crore.
(c) A private company with paid-up capital of ₹20 crore and bank borrowings of ₹55 crore.
(d) A small company.

steps: Rule 5: listed companies; unlisted public companies with paid-up capital ≥ ₹10 crore; private companies with paid-up capital ≥ ₹50 crore; all companies with public borrowings from FIs, banks or public deposits ≥ ₹50 crore.
OPCs and small companies are excluded.
(a) ₹8 crore → out; (b) ₹60 crore private → in; (c) borrowings ₹55 crore → in; (d) small → out.
explanation.formula_used: Rule 5 class: listed / unlisted public ≥ ₹10 cr / private ≥ ₹50 cr / borrowings ≥ ₹50 cr
explanation.trap: The borrowings test catches companies below the capital thresholds.

source_refs.note: Companies Act 2013 s.139(2); Rule 5, Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules 2014

questions.subject: companies-act
questions.microtopic_name: Appointment, rotation and tenure of auditors
questions.stem: CA Harish, an individual, was appointed statutory auditor of Lotus Ltd (listed) at the 2022 AGM until the conclusion of the 2027 AGM. The earliest AGM at which he can again be appointed auditor of Lotus is the:

steps: Individual auditor: only one term of five consecutive years (2022–2027).
Cooling-off: five years from completion of the term → 2032 AGM.
explanation.formula_used: Individual: 1 term of 5 years + 5-year cooling-off; firm: 2 terms + 5 years
explanation.trap: Individuals do not get a second consecutive term.

options.text: 2027 AGM, for a second five-year term
options.error: two-term allowance for firms applied to an individual
options.label: A

questions.subject: companies-act
questions.stem:
Under Rule 6 of the Meetings of Board Rules, which of these unlisted public companies must constitute an Audit Committee (figures per latest audited financial statements)?

| Company | Paid-up capital | Turnover | Outstanding loans, debentures and deposits |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| P | ₹6 crore | ₹120 crore | ₹10 crore |
| Q | ₹9 crore | ₹80 crore | ₹50 crore |
| R | ₹10 crore | ₹30 crore | nil |

steps: Rule 6: paid-up capital ≥ ₹10 crore; OR turnover ≥ ₹100 crore; OR aggregate outstanding loans/borrowings/debentures/deposits exceeding ₹50 crore.
P: turnover ₹120 crore → yes. Q: ₹50 crore does not exceed ₹50 crore; other tests fail → no. R: paid-up ₹10 crore → yes.
explanation.formula_used: Rule 6: ≥ ₹10 cr capital | ≥ ₹100 cr turnover | > ₹50 cr borrowings
explanation.trap: 'Not less than' for capital and turnover, but 'exceeding' for borrowings.

source_refs.note: Companies Act 2013 s.177(1); Rule 6, Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules 2014

options.error: only the paid-up capital test applied
options.label: B

options.error: borrowing test read as '₹50 crore or more' instead of 'exceeding ₹50 crore'
options.label: C

questions.subject: companies-act
questions.stem:
Which of the following are functions of the Audit Committee under s.177(4)?

1. Recommending the appointment, remuneration and terms of appointment of auditors.
2. Approval or any subsequent modification of transactions with related parties.
3. Scrutiny of inter-corporate loans and investments.
4. Making the final appointment of the statutory auditor.

Select the correct answer:

steps: s.177(4): recommend auditors; review independence; examine financial statements; approve/modify RPTs; scrutinise inter-corporate loans and investments; valuation; evaluate internal financial controls; monitor end use of public-offer funds.
The statutory auditor is appointed by the members (s.139(1)).
explanation.formula_used: s.177(4) terms of reference
explanation.trap: The AC recommends; the AGM appoints.

questions.subject: companies-act
questions.stem: A director of Harit Ltd enters into a ₹80 lakh transaction (not covered by s.188) on behalf of the company without the Audit Committee's approval. The Committee does not ratify it within three months. The transaction is:

steps: s.177(4)(iv) proviso: a transaction not exceeding ₹1 crore entered by a director/officer without AC approval and not ratified by the AC within three months is voidable at the AC's option.
₹80 lakh ≤ ₹1 crore; no ratification in 3 months → voidable; the director concerned indemnifies the company for loss if the counterparty is related to him.
explanation.formula_used: s.177(4)(iv): ≤ ₹1 crore, unratified in 3 months → voidable at AC's option
explanation.trap: Voidable, not void — the AC chooses.

options.text: Valid if ratified by the Board at any later date
options.error: Board substituted for the Audit Committee; time limit ignored
options.label: A

options.text: Voidable at the option of the Audit Committee
options.label: C

options.text: Valid, because transactions below ₹1 crore need no Audit Committee approval
options.error: ratification proviso misread as an exemption
options.label: D

questions.subject: companies-act
questions.microtopic_name: Beneficial owner — when a third person qualifies
questions.stem: Under s.89, a person whose name is entered in the register of members but who does not hold the beneficial interest must file a declaration with the company within ____ , and the company must file a return with the Registrar within ____ of receiving it.

steps: s.89(1): registered holder declares within 30 days (MGT-4); s.89(2): beneficial owner declares within 30 days (MGT-5).
s.89(6): company files return with Registrar within 30 days of receipt (MGT-6).
explanation.formula_used: s.89: 30 days / 30 days
explanation.trap: s.89 (nominee holdings) and s.90 (significant beneficial owners) are separate regimes.

options.error: significant beneficial owner transition period confused with s.89
options.label: A

questions.subject: companies-act
questions.microtopic_name: Beneficial owner — when a third person qualifies
questions.stem:
Target Ltd's register shows:

| Member | Holding in Target |
|---|---:|
| Alpha Pvt Ltd | 20% |
| Beta Pvt Ltd | 30% |
| Mr H (directly) | 3% |

Mr H holds 60% of Alpha. Mr K holds 40% of Beta (no one holds a majority of Beta). Neither exercises significant influence or control otherwise. Who is a significant beneficial owner (SBO) of Target?

steps: SBO Rules: an individual holding, directly or indirectly (with direct holdings), not less than 10% of shares/voting/dividend rights, or exercising significant influence or control.
Indirect holding through a company member arises only where the individual holds a majority stake in that member (or its ultimate holding company).
H holds a majority (60%) of Alpha → Alpha's 20% attributed; with direct 3% he crosses 10% → SBO.
K's 40% of Beta is not a majority → no indirect holding → not an SBO.
explanation.formula_used: SBO: ≥ 10% (direct + indirect); indirect via company member only with majority stake
explanation.trap: The rules use a majority-stake gate, not arithmetic multiplication.

source_refs.note: Companies Act 2013 s.90; Companies (Significant Beneficial Owners) Rules 2018, Rule 2(1)(h) and Explanations

options.text: Both Mr H and Mr K
options.error: proportionate look-through used (40% × 30% = 12%) without the majority-stake test
options.label: A

options.text: Neither, since each holds less than 10% directly
options.label: B

questions.subject: companies-act
questions.microtopic_name: Beneficial owner — when a third person qualifies
questions.stem: 15% of the shares of Sagar Ltd are registered in the name of Mr Vikram as trustee of the Asha Family Trust, a discretionary trust settled by Mrs Asha for the benefit of her children. Assuming no other rights, who is treated as holding the right indirectly for SBO purposes?

steps: SBO Rules, Explanation (member is a trust through trustee): trustee — discretionary or charitable trust; beneficiary — specific trust; author/settlor — revocable trust.
Discretionary trust → trustee (Mr Vikram), holding 15% ≥ 10%.
explanation.formula_used: Trust member: discretionary/charitable → trustee; specific → beneficiary; revocable → settlor
explanation.trap: The type of trust decides which third person qualifies.

source_refs.note: Companies (Significant Beneficial Owners) Rules 2018, Rule 2(1)(h) Explanation III(iv)

options.error: revocable-trust rule (author/settlor) applied to a discretionary trust
options.label: A

options.text: No one, because a trust cannot have a significant beneficial owner
options.label: C

questions.subject: companies-act
questions.microtopic_name: Board composition — minimum and maximum directors
questions.stem: The minimum number of directors for a public company, a private company and a One Person Company, and the maximum without a special resolution, are respectively:

steps: s.149(1)(a): minimum 3 (public), 2 (private), 1 (OPC); maximum 15.
More than 15 may be appointed after passing a special resolution.
explanation.formula_used: s.149(1): 3 / 2 / 1; max 15 (more by SR)

questions.stem: The Board of Pranav Ltd, a listed public company, has 11 directors. Under the Companies Act, 2013 (ignore SEBI LODR), the minimum number of independent directors is:

steps: s.149(4): at least one-third of total directors; 11/3 = 3.67.

explanation.formula_used: IDs ≥ ⌈Board ÷ 3⌉ for listed public companies
explanation.trap: Fractions round up, not down.

options.error: Rule 4 minimum for unlisted public companies applied

options.error: one-half requirement of SEBI LODR (executive chairperson) applied

questions.subject: companies-act
questions.microtopic_name: Board composition — minimum and maximum directors
questions.stem:
Aarav Ltd, an unlisted public company, has paid-up capital of ₹60 crore and turnover of ₹320 crore. Consider:

1. Increasing its Board to 17 directors requires a special resolution.
2. It must have at least one woman director.
3. It must have at least one director who stayed in India for at least 182 days in the previous calendar year.

Which are correct?

Rule 3: public companies with paid-up capital ≥ ₹100 crore or turnover ≥ ₹300 crore need a woman director → ₹320 crore → 2 correct.
s.149(3) (as amended 2017): at least one director who stays in India ≥ 182 days during the financial year → 3 wrong.
explanation.formula_used: s.149(1), (3); Rule 3 woman director
explanation.trap: The resident-director test now runs on the financial year.

source_refs.note: Companies Act 2013 s.149(1), s.149(3) (amended 2017); Rule 3, Appointment and Qualification of Directors Rules 2014

options.error: special resolution for more than 15 directors overlooked
options.label: B

options.label: C

questions.stem: The first meeting of the Board of a newly incorporated company must be held within:

steps: s.173(1): first Board meeting within 30 days of incorporation; thereafter at least four meetings a year.
explanation.trap: 180 days is the s.10A declaration window, not the first Board meeting.

questions.microtopic_name: Board meetings — frequency and first meeting timing
questions.stem: Neel Traders Ltd is a small company. Which schedule of Board meetings for calendar year 2026 complies with s.173(5)?

(a) March and September; gap 194 days → compliant.
explanation.formula_used: Small company: one meeting per half-year, ≥ 90 days apart

questions.subject: companies-act
questions.stem:
Which of the following are conditions for a bonus issue under s.63?

**Case — Vellora Engineering Ltd.** Vellora is a listed public company. Its Board has one Managing Director, two Whole-time Directors and four non-executive directors (two of them independent). The statement of profit and loss for FY 2025-26, drawn up **before** charging any managerial remuneration, shows (₹ lakh):

| Item | ₹ lakh |
|---|---:|
| Revenue from operations | 21,500 |
| Subsidy received from the Central Government | 140 |
| Profit on sale of freehold factory land (Vellora does not deal in property) | 420 |
| Unrealised fair-value gain on investments measured at FVTPL | 95 |
| Operating expenses (usual working charges, including staff bonus) | 17,300 |
| Interest on debentures and secured term loans | 480 |
| Depreciation as per Schedule II | 1,050 |
| Loss on sale of a business division (an undertaking) | 210 |
| Ex-gratia payment to a former distributor (no legal liability) | 60 |
| Damages paid under a court decree for breach of contract | 75 |
| Provision for income tax | 700 |

The net profit of Vellora for the purpose of s.197, computed under s.198, is:

explanation.formula_used: s.198 profit = revenue items credited − s.198(4) deductions; capital/fair-value items and income tax ignored

**Case — Sundaram Logistics Ltd.** Sundaram, a public company that is neither a holding nor a subsidiary company, plans to appoint **Rohan Mehta** (who already holds a DIN) as an additional director on 10 November 2026. Rohan is currently a director of 7 public companies, 2 private companies that are subsidiaries of public companies, 6 other private companies and 4 dormant companies, and an alternate director in 1 other private company (not a subsidiary of a public company). An existing Sundaram director, **Leena Rao**, is also a director of Kanak Traders Pvt Ltd, which has not filed its financial statements or annual returns for FY 2022-23, 2023-24 and 2024-25.

Consider Leena Rao's position:

1. She is not eligible to be re-appointed in Kanak, or appointed in any other company, for five years from the date on which Kanak failed to file.
2. Her office as director becomes vacant in Sundaram and also in Kanak.
3. Had Kanak defaulted for only two financial years, s.164(2)(a) would not be attracted.

Which statements are correct?

steps: s.164(2)(a): non-filing of financial statements or annual returns for any continuous period of three FYs → director not eligible for re-appointment in that company or appointment in any other company for five years from the date of failure → 1 correct.
s.167(1)(a) proviso: office vacated in all companies other than the company in default → 2 wrong.
Two years does not satisfy the three-continuous-year trigger → 3 correct.
explanation.formula_used: s.164(2): 3 continuous FYs non-filing → 5-year bar; s.167(1)(a): vacate all except defaulting company
explanation.trap: The defaulting company keeps the director so that it can cure the default.

options.error: vacation extended to the defaulting company itself
options.label: C

steps: s.185(1)(b): no loan to a firm in which a director or his relative is a partner → (i) prohibited.
s.185(2): loan to 'any person in whom the director is interested' (incl. a private company of which he is a member) allowed with special resolution and use for principal business → (ii) permissible.
s.185(3)(a): loan to MD/WTD under a scheme approved by members by special resolution → (iii) permissible.
explanation.formula_used: s.185(1) absolute bar (director, director of holding, partner, firm with director/relative as partner); s.185(2) SR route
explanation.trap: The relative-partner firm is caught by the absolute bar.

source_refs.note: Companies Act 2013 s.185 (as substituted w.e.f. 7 May 2018)

options.error: loan to a private company in which a director is a member treated as absolutely prohibited (pre-2018 view)
options.label: B

options.error: firm in which a director's relative is partner treated as permissible
options.label: C

questions.stem:
**Case — Sundaram Logistics Ltd.** Sundaram, a public company that is neither a holding nor a subsidiary company, plans to appoint **Rohan Mehta** (who already holds a DIN) as an additional director on 10 November 2026. Rohan is currently a director of 7 public companies, 2 private companies that are subsidiaries of public companies, 6 other private companies and 4 dormant companies, and an alternate director in 1 other private company (not a subsidiary of a public company). An existing Sundaram director, **Leena Rao**, is also a director of Kanak Traders Pvt Ltd, which has not filed its financial statements or annual returns for FY 2022-23, 2023-24 and 2024-25.

Which statement about the filings for Rohan's appointment is correct?

steps: s.152(5): a person appointed shall not act unless his consent is filed with the Registrar within 30 days of appointment.
s.170(2): return containing particulars of appointment filed within 30 days.
s.155: an individual holding a DIN shall not obtain another.
explanation.formula_used: Consent (DIR-2) and return (DIR-12) — 30 days each; one DIN for life
explanation.trap: An additional director is a director for every filing purpose.

options.text: Consent and return both to be filed within 60 days of appointment (by 9 January 2027)
options.label: A

options.text: Consent to be filed within 30 days (by 10 December 2026); company's return also within 30 days
options.label: B

options.text: Sundaram must obtain a fresh DIN for Rohan specific to this company before he can act
options.label: C

options.text: No filing is needed, since an additional director holds office only till the next AGM
options.error: additional director treated as outside s.152(5)/s.170(2)
options.label: D
